title: Norm Circles and the Limitations of European Union Normative Projection in Afghanistan
abstract: ABSTRACT Norm diffusion research explains the international travel of norms in semantic terms, through resonance, framing, grafting and localisation. Such accounts presuppose norms to be portable objects whose identity persists through transit. Yet, ontologically, norms exert causal force only where a real social group endorses and enforces them. This article develops Dave Elder‐Vass's critical realist norm‐circle theory into an account of normative projection, recasting ideational travel as a problem of carrier ecology. Explanation turns on which circles operate in the receiving setting, which of them a sponsor can recruit and whether their endorsement and sanction outlast the sponsor's withdrawal. European liberal state‐building in Afghanistan supplies the proof of concept. Retrodicting European engagement from the 1980s to 2021 shows the European Union constituting a distal and imagined circle among governing elites and international audiences while recruiting no proximal circles through which sanction is delivered. Centralising reform had outrun its carriers long before Bonn, from Amanullah in the 1920s to the Soviet‐sponsored reforms of the 1970s. Bonn then conferred status functions without securing enforcers. Gender provisions display the asymmetry most sharply, and the collapse of 2021 exposed rather than produced it. Two amendments to the theory follow. Circles can be spatially disarticulated and differentiated by content, with authority held in international institutions and sanction delivered in the district. Carrier withdrawal operates as a mechanism of normative collapse distinct from contestation or rejection. Normative foreign policy succeeds or fails on the social organisation of enforcement.
